items.title: 71542_Bill Coleman autobiographical manuscript
items.q: Benny had discovered three musicians who were in New York. The pianist, Teddy Wilson... and myself on trumpets... I had heard any number of Earl Hines records... but when I heard Teddy Wilson, I knew that a new star was going to make his footprints in the sands of jazz.

ctx.x: We played a battle of jazz with Zack White's Orchestra in Cincinnati which had as its Director a young alto player named Tremb but better known as Inky because he was so black. I had met Inky some years before in Richmond, Ky., where he was born. I had gone there with Clarence Page and Helvey. Inky had seen Cecil Scott work and had copied the style of wearing a top hat which Cecil and Fess Williams had copied from Ted Lewis. Zack had a very nice orchestra but we were too much for them because we had been together…
We also washed away the orchestra of Speed Webb in a battle of jazz in Cincinnati. Roy Eldridge and Teddy Wilson were in the band but I did not know Teddy then.

Once in Pittsburg we alternated with the Cotton Pickers when they were under the leadership of Don Redman and Joe Smith was in the band. I had been ashamed to take my trumpet case from the bandstand in

items.title: 66600_Teddy Wilson oral history interview
items.q: I had Bill Coleman on trumpet, and Jimmy Hamilton on clarinet

ctx.x: Yeah -- Cadillacs, LaSalles, and in those days before they used to make sports cars, and the old Big wheeling cars. Studebakers back in the old days. You could ride all over New York for a week on a gallon of gas! I remember I had a free wheeling Studebaker.

But anyway, I took the job at the Cafe Society and I did have a great little band there. I had Bill Coleman on trumpet, and Jimmy Hamilton on clarinet -- nobody had ever heard of Jimmy Hamilton in those days, before he went to Duke -- and then Benny Morton on trombone, which was hard to beat; I couldn't afford Benny Morton in my big band, and Al Hall went along with me, though, from my big band on the drums.
